claims.text: The alloy begins service as a single-phase solid solution with uniform composition and microstructure.
Elevated-temperature loading can make the nominally single-phase alloy locally unstable and produce second-phase precipitates or grain-boundary segregation.
High-strain-rate loading can make the alloy locally unstable and produce second-phase precipitates or grain-boundary segregation.
Incipient precipitates or grain-boundary segregation embrittle the alloy and trigger brittle fracture.
Varying temperature and strain rate during fracture testing can induce phase separation or local ordering at grain boundaries.
Exposure to environments that promote embrittling-species uptake can promote diffusion-driven microstructural instability.
Emergent grain-boundary heterogeneities or second-phase nuclei become crack-initiation sites.
Local phase separation or ordering reduces dislocation-based plasticity at grain boundaries.
Reduced grain-boundary plasticity makes grain boundaries susceptible to microcrack formation and propagation under high stress.
Elevated-temperature testing will produce more brittle intergranular cracking than the baseline test.
Elevated-temperature testing will markedly reduce fracture toughness relative to baseline.
High-strain-rate testing will produce more brittle intergranular cracking than the baseline test.
High-strain-rate testing will markedly reduce fracture toughness relative to baseline.
At room temperature and low strain rate, the initial alloy exhibits predominantly ductile fracture behavior.
Service above approximately 700 °C can accelerate diffusion or phase instability sufficiently to enable grain-boundary second-phase formation.
Dynamic stress events can enable second-phase formation at grain boundaries.
The controlled comparison uses the same alloy composition and grain structure while changing temperature or strain rate.
The hypothesis is falsified if elevated temperature or high strain rate produces neither second-phase formation or grain-boundary segregation nor any change in fracture toughness.
